name: Mumaya Sanbonmatsu

location.address: Roadside on National Route 158, Mumaya 633-4, Shokawa-cho, Takayama, Gifu Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, no permission needed. Stands directly beside National Route 158, about 1.5km from Matsunoki Pass toward Hirugano Highland; visible from the road with no gate or entry restriction.
transport: No rail connection; by car, roughly 45-55 minutes from central Takayama via Route 158 (or continue about 10-15 minutes further along Route 158 from Shokawa-zakura Park).
verify_notes: NOT three separate pines despite the name: hitozato-kyoboku.com (photographed 2022-10-15, citing the Environment Agency giant-tree survey, Tokai edition, 1988 report) describes ONE Japanese red pine that splits into three trunks about 2 metres above ground, the branching point resembling Neptune/Poseidon's trident. This is a single collectible specimen, not a grove or avenue. Two sources give slightly different figures: hitozato (1988 survey) records height 21m, girth (breast-height) 3.5m, age 300+ years; Takayama City's own current natural-monument list gives girth 3.3m and age approximately 320 years, address Takayama-shi, Shokawa-cho, Mumaya 633-4. Designated a Takayama City natural monument on 1971-10-13 (per hitozato, citing the on-site marker; the modern city list does not repeat the date). Coordinates converted from hitozato's stated 36 03 41.7N 137 02 27.9E match the candidate coordinates exactly. Stands right on the shoulder of Route 158, described by the surveyor as vigorous with full foliage on all three trunks to the crown. Joins Shokawa (sho_001, the Shokawa-zakura, 8.7km away along the same National Route 158), same rural car-access pattern already used for that entry; no public transport serves either site.

name: Ito Hirobumi Memorial Camphor

location.address: Oyamazumi Shrine, Miyaura, Omishima, Imabari, Ehime Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, within the grounds of Oyamazumi Shrine, open daily.
transport: On Omishima Island (Shimanami Kaido); same access as the shrine's other published tree (omi_001, Ikiki no Gomon), a few hundred metres away within the same shrine precinct.
verify_notes: Documented planting date, not a derived estimate: Ito Hirobumi, Japan's first Prime Minister, planted this camphor himself on 1909-03-22 (Meiji 42) to mark a pilgrimage visit to Oyamazumi Shrine, the same visit in which he personally wrote the shrine's stone name-tablet (sha-go-hyo). Two independent sources agree on the date and give the same trunk girth, roughly 1m (young/slender by the standards of this shrine's ancient camphors). Ito is traditionally said to be a descendant of the Kono clan, whose tutelary shrine this is, which is the stated reason for his visit. NOT individually a National Natural Monument: the shrine's designation (1951, 'Japan's oldest primeval camphor grove', 38 named ancient camphors) covers the old sacred trees; this one is a modern (117-year) memorial planting within the same grounds and is not one of the 38. Included here on historical significance (a Prime Minister's own commemorative tree, verifiable planting date) rather than age or girth, per the qualifying test 'genuinely old OR visually spectacular OR historically significant'. Alive and current: 2024-dated photographs of the shrine grounds exist online (jalan.net and others); the shrine is a major, constantly-visited tourist site so an undocumented death is very unlikely. location_precision set approximate: no source gives tree-level coordinates for this specific planting distinct from the shrine's own address; the coordinate given is the shrine's. IMPORTANT: do not confuse with Kono Michiari's helmet-hanging camphor (see blocked list), a different, unrelated and long-dead tree at the same shrine.

name: Ushio no Katsura

location.address: Nihara Shrine (Hinohara Jinja) approach steps, Kaishio (Ushio), Daito-cho, Unnan, Shimane Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, on the grounds of Nihara Shrine (owner/manager of record); stands beside the shrine's approach stone steps, open to the public.
transport: Rural Unnan City, Shimane Prefecture; by car only, no direct train or confirmed bus. About 22km / an estimated 30-35 minute drive from Okuizumo's own tree (okz_001, Takezaki no Katsura), which is itself reached by car with no public transport.
verify_notes: Real Japanese name is Kaishio (Ushio) no Katsura (海潮のカツラ), not simply Ushio; Kaishio/Ushio is the district name in Daito-cho, Unnan City. National Natural Monument since 1937-04-17 (bunka.go.jp designation #212), one of two independent sources; ja.wikipedia corroborates species, shrine ownership and location. Base girth reported as approximately 13m by the official bunka.go.jp record; a separate source (rekishi-king.com) gives an even larger root-girth figure of about 18m and a height near 40m against bunka.go.jp's 30m, likely because this is a multi-trunk specimen (the main trunk has rotted away and 7 secondary trunks now rise from the base), so any single girth figure describes the base cluster rather than one trunk; recorded girth_cm 1300 from the official record and flagged the discrepancy for the writer. No documented planting or origin date exists in any source found; a local tourism blog title calls it 'a thousand-year giant tree' but that reads as informal description rather than a sourced age claim, so age_estimate is left not documented rather than repeating that figure. Local legend/feature: a 'mirror rock' (kagami-iwa) near the shrine is said to reflect the tree, per the rekishi-king.com piece; worth checking further for the story. Distance note for the container decision: Okuizumo's own page already treats its one tree as car-only rural access with no public transport claimed, so a ~30 minute drive to a second katsura of this stature is consistent with how that page already presents itself; equally, a National Monument since 1937 with a base girth this large could clear the single-tree-destination bar on its own merits (own-place candidate, Kaishio/Ushio, Unnan) if Hidde or the write pass prefers that over joining Okuizumo. Recording both options rather than forcing one.

name: Yashiro-no-Okeyaki

location.address: Ashika Shrine (Ashika Jinja) grounds, at the foot of Mount Babayama, Yashiro, Asago, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, within the grounds of Ashika Shrine, open to the public.
transport: Rural Asago/Yabu border area, Hyogo Prefecture; no train or bus stop confirmed. Straight-line distance is 8.8km from Yabu's yab_002 (Takinoya no Hidarimakigaya) and 14.5km from yab_001, both closer than the 23.4km to Asago's own published tree (asg_001) in Itoi Gorge; despite the administrative address being Asago City, the geography argues for joining Yabu rather than Asago.
verify_notes: Two independent sources agree closely. bunka.go.jp (the official national register, designated 1928-03-24): root circumference ~17.6m, girth at the base-root boundary ~12.7m, trunk circumference 1.5m above the base ~8.1m, height ~27m (at time of designation). tanshin-kikin.jp (a Tajima-region local heritage encyclopedia): height now about 20m, trunk circumference 8.1m (matching bunka.go.jp's upper measurement exactly), age estimated at 'a thousand and some hundred years' (recorded here broadly as 1000-1900 to avoid false precision). Real name of the shrine is Ashika Jinja (足鹿神社), not to be confused with Ashikaga; stands at the foot of Mount Babayama. History: at the time of its 1928 designation the tree stood about 30m tall and was called the finest zelkova in the prefecture; since then typhoon damage and nearby shrine-ground construction have hollowed the trunk and reduced its height to about 20m, though the main trunk and root system are described as retaining their majestic character and it remains the town's symbol. Asago City carried out major national/prefecturally-subsidised restoration work in 1988 and has continued trunk-preservation efforts since, a good 'witnessed and was saved' story beat. IMPORTANT for the container decision: this tree's official address is Yashiro, Asago City, but its coordinates (confirmed via Commons category, matching the candidate's exactly) place it 8.8km from Yabu's yab_002 and only 14.5km from yab_001, against 23.4km to Asago's own published tree (asg_001, in Itoi Gorge, a different and distant part of a large rural municipality). Recommend joining Yabu on geography despite the administrative name; Asago remains the technically correct place name for the address field.

name: Kuchioya no O-Abemaki

location.address: Naka, Oya-cho, Yabu City, Hyogo Prefecture, Japan (hillside behind a former school)
location.neighbourhood: Oya-cho, Yabu City, about 0.8km from Tarumi-no-Ozakura (yab_001)

access: Free, locally revered as a sacred tree; stands on a mountainside behind a former school. No confirmed parking or maintained path noted by the local tourism board, but no restriction or gate mentioned either.
transport: Oya-cho, Yabu City, Hyogo Prefecture; no train or bus stop confirmed. Only about 0.8km from Yabu's own published Tarumi-no-Ozakura (yab_001), easily the closest joinder of this batch.
verify_notes: National Natural Monument designated 1951-06-09 (per bunka.nii.ac.jp / national register). Girth 5.6m, height approximately 16m, estimated age approximately 400 years, per the official register; the Yabu tourism association's own page (yabu-kankou.jp) repeats the same three figures independently and adds that this is considered a rare giant example of Abemaki (Quercus variabilis) in Japan, and that it is locally regarded as a sacred dwelling place of the gods (goshintai-like reverence) rather than a shrine tree specifically. Coordinates from the Commons category (35.343, 134.70672) match the candidate's almost exactly. No dated recent photo or news confirming current vitality was found beyond the tourism board's current listing, which reads as an actively maintained attraction rather than a stale record; flagged rather than fully certain on 'alive now' evidence for that reason. Very close to Yabu's existing Tarumi-no-Ozakura (0.8km), making this the easiest addition of the whole batch and a natural pairing on the same short walk/drive.

name: Shinmeisha no Oshii

location.address: Kaminagara Shinmeisha shrine, Kaminagara-cho, Nishio, Aichi Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, standing directly in front of the main hall of Kaminagara Shinmeisha shrine, open to the public.
transport: In Nishio, Aichi Prefecture; nearest existing published city is roughly 35km away (per the demand tool), too far for a day-trip addition, so this is an own-place candidate under the 2026-08-31 single-tree exception.
verify_notes: SPECIES CORRECTION: an automated page-fetch of the national register mistranslated the species as a camphor tree; the Japanese source text and the Commons category both name it Castanopsis sieboldii (sudajii/itajii), an evergreen chinquapin oak, not Cinnamomum camphora. Do not repeat the camphor mistranslation. National Natural Monument, designated 1932-04-19. Two independent Japanese sources agree closely: root circumference 20m, trunk girth at breast height 7m (bunka.go.jp gives approximately 8m for the same measurement point, a minor register discrepancy, both recorded), height 8m, estimated age about 1,000 years. Described as the largest sudajii in Aichi Prefecture. IMPORTANT HONESTY POINT, not a reason to block: the ORIGINAL MAIN TRUNK has died. The tree survives today, per both the national register and the city tourism board's current listing, through two secondary branch-trunks of about 1m girth each plus root suckers sprouting around the base, described as currently thriving and extending upward. This reads as the same kind of living-succession case as the Elm of Saint-Gervais precedent (a dead original honestly succeeded by living growth from the same base), not as a dead stump like Kono Michiari's camphor (see blocked list on this same pass): the difference is the description is present-tense and continuous, not a historical account of something removed. Deliver as alive, flagged, with the dead-main-trunk fact stated plainly for the story. Single-tree-destination test: passes on the combination of a c.1,000-year estimated age, National Natural Monument status since 1932, and the record-holder claim of largest sudajii in the prefecture; Nishio has no published city page yet, so this would open as its own place (id prefix suggestion: nis, or a Kaminagara/Shinmeisha-based slug).

name: Sugimori Jinja no Ohatsuki Icho

location.address: Sugimori Shrine, Rikurodani, Takahama, Oi District, Fukui Prefecture, Japan

access: Free, within the grounds of Sugimori Shrine, open to the public.
transport: In Takahama, Fukui Prefecture, on the Wakasa Bay coast; nearest existing published city is roughly 51km away per the demand tool, too far for a day-trip addition, so this is an own-place candidate under the 2026-08-31 single-tree exception.
verify_notes: This is a COMPACT PAIR under one designation, not one tree, and it passes the collectible-point test as an ensemble rather than as a single specimen: one National Natural Monument (designated 1935-08-27) covers TWO female ginkgo trees standing a short distance apart within the small grounds of Sugimori Shrine, one on the eastern hillside behind the main hall (girth about 3m) and one on the western side in front of it (girth about 2.8m), both roughly 32m tall. Both are the rare 'ohatsuki' variety, a genetic trait in which seed-like structures (ovules) form directly on the leaf margins instead of on normal branches, which is what earned the national designation ('academically valuable', per the register) rather than age or size; only a handful of such designated ohatsuki ginkgos exist in Japan (others include Nanaho, Ibaraki's Shirahatayama Hachimangu, and Soda per the search results, so this is a genuinely rare botanical curiosity, not a generic old ginkgo). No age is documented anywhere found; leave age_estimate empty rather than guess, and let the story lead with the leaf-fruiting trait instead. Two independent sources (the national register text and ja.wikipedia, which cites the same register) agree on designation date, species and both trees' existence and rough measurements. Coordinates from the Commons category (35.483167, 135.474722) match the candidate exactly; this points at the shrine grounds generally rather than pinning either specific trunk, so treat the pin as shrine-level. Recommend as its own place (Takahama, Fukui, or a Sugimori-Jinja/Rikurodani slug); Takahama has no published city page.

name: Kagoji no Shibunashigaya
species: Seedless-astringency Kaya / Japanese Nutmeg-yew (Torreya nucifera, shibunashi variant)

location.address: Kagoji Temple, Nishiyama 1182, Iga City, Mie Prefecture, Japan
location.neighbourhood: Nishiyama, Iga City, about 1km from Takakura Shrine (iga_001)

access: Free, in the northeastern part of Kagoji Temple's grounds; parking and restrooms available on site.
transport: About 15 minutes by taxi from Iga Tetsudo's Ueno-shi Station, or about 15 minutes by car from the Meishin Expressway's Ouchi IC. About 1km from Iga's already-published Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya (iga_001).
verify_notes: This is a SECOND, DISTINCT tree from the already-published iga_001 (Takakura Jinja no Shibunashigaya), not a duplicate: different site (Kagoji Temple vs Takakura Shrine), 1.0km apart, and iga_001's own published story already states that only two or three shibunashigaya trees hold national designation anywhere in Japan (a third was delisted after it died), which this pass confirms: this is the sibling National Natural Monument. Same rare cultivar as iga_001, a variant of Torreya nucifera (kaya) whose kernels lack the normal astringent skin, historically valuable in the Edo period for cooking oil and for a sugar-coated confection (kaya arare) made in Iga and Kiso. Girth at 50cm above ground is 370cm; the trunk forks into three main limbs around 90cm up; canopy spreads about 15m east-west by 18m north-south; height about 20m. Described as vigorous and fruiting heavily every year in late summer, which is good recent-vitality evidence even without a dated photo. National Natural Monument (exact designation date not confirmed this pass; both Mie tourism board and ja.wikipedia cite the same national register without repeating the date on the pages fetched) plus a place on Mie Prefecture's own '100 Selected Trees' list. No age documented in any source found. Given the two Iga shibunashigaya are administratively and physically close (1km) and share one very specific, rare identity (one of only 2-3 in the whole country), the write pass may want to tell their two stories together rather than duplicate the varietal explanation on both pages.

name: Kozoji no Kotsubugaya
species: Small-seed Kaya / Japanese Nutmeg-yew (Torreya nucifera, kotsubugaya variant)

location.address: Kozoji Temple grove, Kawachi-cho, Toba, Mie Prefecture, Japan

access: Within the temple grove (jusou) of Kozoji Temple; visiting details available via Toba City's Lifelong Learning Division. No indication of restricted access; treat as open grounds.
transport: In Kawachi-cho, Toba, Mie Prefecture; nearest existing published city is roughly 47km away per the demand tool, too far for a day-trip addition, so this is an own-place candidate under the 2026-08-31 single-tree exception.
verify_notes: UNIT CORRECTION: an automated page-fetch rendered the 4.5m figure as 'diameter at breast height', but the Japanese source text says girth/circumference at breast height (mune-dori miki-shu 4.5m / me-dori-miki-i 4.5m), not diameter; recorded correctly here as girth_cm 450. Height 25m; the crown tip was lost to a lightning strike at some point but the tree's vigour is described as still robust (both the city and a 2026-vintage web summary agree). Rarity is the whole story: kotsubugaya is a native Japanese varietal of kaya (Torreya nucifera) whose seeds, including the aril, run only 18-20mm across, distinctly smaller than ordinary kaya seed. This specimen was first locally designated a Toba City natural monument on 1970-03-24 as simply a fine old kaya; a 1991 (Heisei 3) survey identified it as only the SECOND known kotsubugaya in Japan (the first being one in Miyagi Prefecture, Ohara no Kotsubugaya), which is what earned it promotion to a National Natural Monument, formally designated 1993-01-20 (Heisei 5). Two independent sources (Toba City's own heritage page and ja.wikipedia, which cites the national register) agree on the measurements and the designation history. No age is documented in any source found. Toba has no published city page; recommend as its own place given the national designation and the genuine national-level rarity (one of only two known trees of this variant in the country).
